sandbox.title: Physics sandbox
sandbox.subtitle: Run isolated Newtonian experiments. Each preset resets to its own exact initial state.
sandbox.impactEnergyModelled: Estimated from the catalogue impact speed before the collision.
sandbox.impactEnergyActual: Recalculated from the simulated impact speed.
sandbox.airburstFlag: The impact module heuristic flags possible airburst conditions.
sandbox.airburstUnsupported: The gas giant has no solid-surface model; atmospheric burst effects are not estimated.
sandbox.noAirburstFlag: The impact module heuristic does not flag airburst conditions.

validity.valid: Far-field range: Newtonian approximation marked valid by the model gauge.
validity.caution: Caution: Newtonian approximation is increasingly limited here.
validity.invalid: Outside the stated range of the Newtonian approximation.

notes.stable: JPL Solar System initial conditions, integrated with the app's fixed-step Newtonian engine.
notes.twoBody: Sun and Earth initial state from JPL; other bodies are omitted for this two-body experiment.
notes.impact: Earth and a 500 m radius, 3000 kg/m³ illustrative asteroid. Impact energy and the airburst flag use the impact module. The N-body engine does not resolve body contact, an atmospheric trajectory, or damage.
notes.starReplacement: Instantly replaces the Sun's gravitational parameter with half its initial value while preserving all positions and velocities. This is a controlled thought experiment, not stellar evolution.
notes.blackHole: A 1000 solar-mass non-rotating black hole and a test particle at 12 Schwarzschild radii. Newtonian particle motion is only an approximation; see the validity gauge.
notes.empty: An empty simulation clock with no bodies. Conservation diagnostics are undefined.

sandbox.starModelCard: Model Card · Instantaneous mass substitution. Other bodies keep their positions and velocities. No stellar evolution, mass loss, ejecta, or radiation is modelled.
sandbox.blackHoleModelCard: Model Card · Non-rotating Schwarzschild geometry for radius and gauge; test-particle trajectory remains Newtonian. No relativistic trajectory or light propagation.
sandbox.impactModelCard: Model Card · Spherical uniform-density impactor and Newtonian kinetic energy. Body contact is not resolved. Airburst output is a coarse heuristic, not a probability or damage forecast.
sandbox.newtonianModelCard: Model Card · Point-mass Newtonian gravity with a fixed-step velocity-Verlet integrator. Scene geometry is illustrative and not to scale.
sandbox.assumptions: Assumed because the record has no value: {list}.
sandbox.unverified: Catalogue values are approximate and unverified.
sandbox.catalogNote: Scenario built from the catalogue record. It uses the same simplified Newtonian engine as the presets; see the model card below for limits.
sandbox.collisionBody: The body reached {target} after {days} d at {speed} km/s. The run is stopped; press reset to repeat.

lab.title: Simulation labs
lab.subtitle: Pick a model, then run it with a preset or with an object from the catalogue.

star-replacement.title: Star replacement
star-replacement.body: Swap the Sun for another star mass and watch whether the planets stay bound.
star-replacement.limit: Newtonian gravity only: no stellar evolution, no luminosity or climate model.

impact.title: Impact
impact.body: Send an asteroid or comet at Earth: kinetic energy, TNT equivalent, airburst flag, and a stop when the body reaches Earth.
impact.limit: No crater, blast or casualty model; energy figures are a simple kinetic estimate.

black-hole.title: Black hole
black-hole.body: Orbit a test particle around a black hole at 12 Schwarzschild radii, with a validity gauge for the Newtonian approximation.
black-hole.limit: Newtonian approximation, not general relativity; no lensing, no spin.

sandbox.title: Build your own
sandbox.body: Place your own bodies and watch them orbit; energy and angular-momentum drift are shown live.
sandbox.limit: Planar start, point masses, no collisions between your bodies.

scale.label: Scale
scale.galaxyNote: 1 unit = 500 light-years. Directions and distances of listed objects are real; the spiral arms are illustrative, not a measured map.
scale.universeNote: Directions are real; distances are compressed and galaxy sizes exaggerated so everything fits. Not to scale.

gallery.title: Experiments you can run right now
gallery.subtitle: Pick a ready-made scenario and it opens in the simulator immediately. Every value comes from the catalog and is labelled as an estimate; nothing here is a prediction.
gallery.communityEmpty: Nobody has published an experiment yet. Save one in the sandbox and share it.
gallery.communityOffline: Community experiments are unavailable right now (database not connected). The ready-made ones above work normally.

stable-system.title: Stable Solar System
stable-system.body: Sun and planets from real initial conditions. Watch energy and angular momentum stay constant.

two-body.title: Two-body problem
two-body.body: Two bodies orbiting a common centre of mass. The cleanest test of the integrator.

star-replacement.title: Replace the Sun
star-replacement.body: Swap the Sun for another star and see which planets keep their orbits and which fly away.

asteroid-impact.title: Asteroid on a collision course
asteroid-impact.body: Launch an asteroid at Earth and read impact speed, energy in TNT and airburst/crater outcome.

black-hole.title: Black-hole flyby
black-hole.body: A test particle near a Newtonian black hole (approximation, no relativity). Orbit, plunge or escape.

chelyabinsk-2013.body: 19 m airburst over Russia, about 500 kt. Compare the energy the simulator computes with the published figure.

tunguska-1908.body: Siberian airburst that flattened forest. Size and speed are highly uncertain, shown as such.

chicxulub.body: The end-Cretaceous impact. Energy is order-of-magnitude only; see how large that is next to the others.

apophis.body: Near-Earth asteroid with a safe 2029 flyby. Orbit from catalog values; no collision is predicted.

halley.body: Highly eccentric comet (e≈0.97). Speed changes enormously between perihelion and aphelion.

sirius-a.body: Put a 2-solar-mass A star at the centre. Which planets survive, and how do the periods change?

betelgeuse.body: Replace the Sun with a red supergiant. Its mass is uncertain; the sandbox warns about planets inside it.

proxima-centauri.body: A 0.12 solar-mass red dwarf has too little gravity to hold the Solar System planets.

cygnus-x-1.body: Stellar-mass black hole of about 21 solar masses. Test particle orbits, Newtonian approximation.

sagittarius-a-star.body: The Milky Way’s central black hole, about 4 million solar masses. Orbits are fast and tight.

m87-star.body: A 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole. An extreme gravitational parameter for the engine.

proxima-b.body: Planet in an 11-day orbit. Minimum mass only; see how fast it moves around its small star.

51-pegasi-b.body: The first hot Jupiter: a giant planet orbiting in 4 days at 0.05 AU.

trappist-1e.body: Rocky planet around an ultracool dwarf. A 6-day year at a tiny orbital distance.

55-cancri-e.body: Lava world orbiting in under a day. A very fast, tight orbit.

mission.title: Space Mission Design Game
mission.intro: Plan a real-feeling space mission from idea to final report. Every choice costs mass, power, money, or time, and there is rarely one perfect answer.

mass.label: Mass
mass.help: Fully fuelled spacecraft against what the rocket can lift to this destination.

power.label: Power
power.help: Average electrical load against average power, counting time in shadow.

budget.label: Budget
budget.help: Building, launching, and operating the mission against the funds you have.

data.label: Data
data.help: Data made each day against what the radio can send home each day.

time.label: Time
time.help: The launch month against the deadline. Planets only line up for departure at certain times.

science.label: Science
science.help: Best possible science from these instruments in this orbit, against the goal. More is better.

objective.title: Choose your mission
objective.help: Start with the question you want answered. The objective sets your budget, deadline, and science goal.

earth-climate.name: Watch Earth's climate
earth-climate.brief: Track ice, oceans, and heat from orbit for at least two years.

moon-ice.name: Find ice on the Moon
moon-ice.brief: Map water ice in the dark craters near the lunar poles.

mars-water.name: Search for water on Mars
mars-water.brief: Use radar to look for ice buried under the surface of Mars.

jupiter-magnetosphere.name: Explore Jupiter's magnetic field
jupiter-magnetosphere.brief: Measure the strongest magnetic field of any planet, through intense radiation.

team.title: Who is playing?
team.signoff: Team sign-off: all four roles must agree to launch

director.name: Mission director
director.duty: Pick the objective and protect the budget.
director.goal: Goal: keep at least 10% of the budget unspent.

engineer.name: Systems engineer
engineer.duty: Build a spacecraft that survives the mission.
engineer.goal: Goal: at least 10% mass margin and 15% power margin.

scientist.name: Science lead
scientist.duty: Choose instruments that answer the mission's question.
scientist.goal: Goal: return 20% more science than the mission requires.

operator.name: Flight operations lead
operator.duty: Choose the orbit and rocket, and plan how data gets home.
operator.goal: Goal: bring home at least 80% of the collected data.

spacecraft.title: Build the spacecraft
spacecraft.help: Watch the resource panel as you choose. Each upgrade helps one system and costs another.

extras.bus: Carries {payload} kg of instruments, {tank} kg of fuel

payload.title: Choose scientific instruments
payload.help: More instruments mean more science, but also more mass, power, cost, and data to send home.

orbit.title: Choose orbit and launch vehicle
orbit.help: The orbit decides what you can see, how much fuel you burn, and how much sun you get. The rocket must be able to carry you there.
orbit.derived: One orbit: {period} min · in shadow: {eclipse} min · fuel: {propellant} kg for {deltaV} m/s
orbit.lifetimeHelp: A longer mission returns more data, but needs more fuel and operations money.

bus-small.name: Small bus
bus-small.desc: Light and cheap, but with little room.

bus-medium.name: Medium bus
bus-medium.desc: A balanced frame for most missions.

bus-large.name: Large bus
bus-large.desc: Holds a lot, but is heavy and slow to build.

solar-2.name: Small solar array
solar-2.desc: Enough near Earth for a small spacecraft.

solar-6.name: Medium solar array
solar-6.desc: A good fit for Earth, Moon, and light Mars missions.

solar-60.name: Giant solar array
solar-60.desc: Sunlight at Jupiter is 27 times weaker, so size matters.

rtg.name: Radioisotope generator
rtg.desc: Nuclear heat gives steady power with no sunlight, at a high price.

battery-small.name: Small battery
battery-small.desc: For short eclipses and light loads.

battery-medium.name: Medium battery
battery-medium.desc: Carries a typical spacecraft through shadow.

comms-small.name: Small antenna
comms-small.desc: Fine close to Earth, too weak for deep space.

comms-medium.name: Medium dish
comms-medium.desc: A strong link out to the Moon.

comms-large.name: Large dish
comms-large.desc: Good for the inner solar system.

comms-deep.name: Deep-space dish
comms-deep.desc: A big high-power dish for Mars and beyond.

computer-basic.name: Basic computer
computer-basic.desc: Cheap, with little memory and little radiation protection.

adcs-magnetic.name: Magnetic torquers
adcs-magnetic.desc: Push against Earth's magnetic field. Rough pointing, Earth orbit only.

adcs-redundant.name: Redundant wheels
adcs-redundant.desc: A spare wheel keeps pointing precise after a failure.

prop-cold.name: Cold gas thrusters
prop-cold.desc: Simple and light, but very inefficient.

prop-biprop.name: Bipropellant engine
prop-biprop.desc: Heavier, but needs far less fuel for big burns.

camera-hires.name: High-resolution camera
camera-hires.desc: Sharp detail, large images, and precise pointing needed.

spectrometer.name: Imaging spectrometer
spectrometer.desc: Reads what surfaces are made of from their light.

radar.name: Sounding radar
radar.desc: Sees beneath the surface, but is heavy and power hungry.

laser-altimeter.name: Laser altimeter
laser-altimeter.desc: Maps the height of the terrain.

magnetometer.name: Magnetometer
magnetometer.desc: Measures magnetic fields. Tiny and efficient.

particle-detector.name: Particle detector
particle-detector.desc: Counts charged particles around the spacecraft.

leo-sso.name: Sun-synchronous orbit, 700 km
leo-sso.desc: Passes over the whole Earth at the same local time each day.

leo-low.name: Low orbit, 450 km
leo-low.desc: Closer views, but air drag costs fuel and the poles are missed.

geo.name: Geostationary orbit, 35,786 km
geo.desc: Always above one spot, far from fine detail.

llo-polar.name: Low polar lunar orbit, 100 km
llo-polar.desc: Sees all of the Moon, including the poles. Needs regular corrections.

lunar-elliptic.name: Elliptical lunar orbit
lunar-elliptic.desc: Less fuel and stable, with less coverage and detail.

mars-low-polar.name: Low polar Mars orbit, 400 km
mars-low-polar.desc: Sees the whole planet, but needs a big braking burn.

mars-elliptic.name: Elliptical Mars orbit
mars-elliptic.desc: Half the braking fuel, with much less coverage and detail.

jupiter-polar.name: Polar Jupiter orbit
jupiter-polar.desc: Close passes over the poles through extreme radiation.

jupiter-distant.name: Distant Jupiter orbit
jupiter-distant.desc: Gentler radiation, but sees much less.

review.title: Launch review
review.help: Blocking problems must be fixed. Warnings can fly, but you will see their effect in orbit.
review.clear: No problems found. The mission is go for launch.

issues.noInstruments: A spacecraft with no instruments cannot do any science. Add at least one.
issues.busPayload: Instruments weigh {used} kg, but this bus carries {limit} kg. Pick a bigger bus or fewer instruments.
issues.propellantImpossible: This engine cannot deliver {deltaV} m/s: with an efficiency of {isp} s, the tanks could never hold enough fuel. Pick a more efficient engine.
issues.tankOverflow: The mission needs {used} kg of fuel, but the tanks hold {limit} kg. A more efficient engine or a bigger bus would fix it.
issues.launcherCannotReach: This rocket cannot reach the destination. Pick a more powerful one.
issues.launcherOverweight: The spacecraft weighs {used} kg, but this rocket lifts {limit} kg here. Lose mass or pick a bigger rocket.
issues.overBudget: The mission costs ${used}M, but you have ${limit}M. Parts, the rocket, and operations all count.
issues.lateLaunch: The launch falls in month {used}, after the month {limit} deadline. Fewer or simpler instruments and a smaller bus are faster to build.
issues.magneticAwayFromEarth: Magnetic torquers need Earth's magnetic field, so they cannot work at this destination. Use reaction wheels.
issues.needsFinePointing: An instrument needs precise pointing that magnetic torquers cannot give. Use reaction wheels.
issues.shortLifetime: A {used}-month mission is shorter than the {limit} months required.
issues.missingCapability: The mission's main question needs {missing}. Without it, the science value falls sharply.
issues.powerDeficit: The spacecraft needs {used} W but gets only {limit} W on average, so instruments will often be switched off.
issues.thinPower: Power margin is only {margin}%. A little panel damage could shut down instruments.
issues.batteryShort: Getting through the shadow takes {used} Wh, but the battery can safely give {limit} Wh. Instruments will pause in eclipse.
issues.downlinkShort: Instruments make {used} Gb per day, but the radio can send only {limit} Gb. The rest may be lost.
issues.radiationExposure: Radiation here is {radiation}%, but the computer tolerates {tolerance}%. It may fail suddenly.
issues.lowScience: Even a perfect flight gives {used} science points, and the goal is {limit}.

flight.noWebgl: 3D view is not available in this browser. The mission still runs below.
flight.notToScale: Illustration, not to scale. The transfer path uses a real Hohmann ellipse.

events.launchFailure: The rocket failed during ascent. Even reliable rockets carry risk.
events.separation: The spacecraft separated from the rocket.
events.insertion: Braking burn of {deltaV} m/s complete. In orbit.
events.insertionFailure: The braking burn failed and the spacecraft missed its orbit.
events.solarFlare: Solar flare! Safe mode for {days} days.
events.micrometeoroid: A micrometeoroid hit the solar panels: {loss}% of power lost.
events.wheelFailure: A reaction wheel failed. Precise instruments now work {duty}% of the time.
events.wheelFailover: A reaction wheel failed, and the spare took over with no science lost.
events.groundOutage: Ground station outage: no contact for {days} days. Data waits in memory.
events.radiationKill: Radiation destroyed the onboard computer. Contact lost.
events.powerCollapse: Power fell to {available} W, below the {needed} W needed to survive. Contact lost.
events.transmitterFade: The transmitter has aged: only {left}% of the data rate is left.

report.summary: Worked for {days} of {planned} planned days, sent home {returned} Gb, science {science} of {required} required.
report.why: Why it turned out this way
report.redesign: Change the design and fly again

insights.launchFailure: The rocket failed. It was bad luck, not bad design, and real programmes plan for it with insurance and spare hardware.
insights.insertionFailure: The braking burn failed on arrival. Every mission has moments with no second chance.
insights.radiationKill: The computer died after {days} of {planned} days. Radiation-hardened electronics cost more, but this orbit demands them.
insights.powerCollapse: After {days} of {planned} days, power fell below what the spacecraft needs to stay alive. Add panels or cut the load.
insights.missingCapability: The mission lacked {missing}, so it could not answer its main question.
insights.dataLost: {pct}% of the data was lost: instruments made {generated} Gb per day, but the radio sent only {downlink} Gb. Signal strength falls with the square of distance, so a bigger dish or more power helps. So does collecting less.
insights.dataHealthy: The communications system kept up, and {pct}% of the data was kept.
insights.lowDuty: Instruments ran only {pct}% of the time because power or safe mode stopped them. More power or a smaller load would help.
insights.batteryShort: Each {eclipse}-minute eclipse needed {need} Wh, but the battery could safely give {have} Wh, so instruments paused in shadow.
insights.powerMargin: A {pct}% power margin kept the spacecraft safe when panels wore out or got damaged.
insights.budgetMargin: You kept {pct}% of the budget in reserve. Real missions need this for surprises.
insights.scienceShort: Science reached {value} of the {required} required. Better instruments, a better orbit, or more data returned would raise it.
insights.redundancyPaid: The spare reaction wheel paid for itself: a failure did not cost any science.
insights.noRedundancy: A wheel failed with no spare. Redundancy adds mass and cost, but protects the science.
insights.launchWindow: The spacecraft was ready early and waited {months} months for the planets to line up. The team's salaries still had to be paid.

tutorial.title: How to play
tutorial.one: Pick a mission. It sets your budget, deadline, and science goal.
tutorial.two: Build the spacecraft and watch the resources panel: every part costs something.
tutorial.three: Choose instruments, an orbit, and a rocket, then pass the launch review.
tutorial.four: Fly it, read why it worked or failed, change the design, and try for a better score.

sandbox.label: Sandbox mode
sandbox.help: Experiment with no budget or schedule limit. Scores are not ranked.
